newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open firm before jobless, housing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open firm before jobless, housing.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened slightly higher on Thursday ahead of June housing starts data and the weekly jobless claims report.
Economists polled by Reuters, on average, said they expected new jobless claims to fall back to 345,000 for the week ended July 12 from the prior week's surge to 377,000.

Economists linked the numerous new claims filed in the week ended July 5 to auto plant planned shutdowns as factories retool for new models. They said they expect jobless claims levels to be volatile in July and even in early August.
Economists told Reuters that housing starts in June should have risen to an approximate annualized rate of 1.45 million, up from 1.397 million in May, helped by lower borrowing costs.
Improved weather conditions might also have helped to boost starts in June, they said, after a rainy season damped construction activity in May.
Both the jobless claims and housing data are due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Analysts said the market would also take note of the Philadelphia Federal Reserve's survey of regional business conditions.
The Philadelphia Fed's survey is of July activity and is therefore quite current, they noted. Economists project a reading of 18 for the survey, down from 25.2 in June.

"The big feature today will be housing starts," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Securities. "The jobless claims numbers will be hard to interpret over the next weeks due to the summer auto plant shutdowns and how the Labor Department will be adjusting the seasonals for that."
Flanagan said the Philadelphia Fed report would also attract attention.
But he said bond prices lately have not reacted that much to the report.
"Perhaps people feel it's too local," he said.
The Treasury will sell $13.0 billion in 52-week bills at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT, an auction that is not expected to cause any problems for the market.
Analysts said the market's attention would start to shift toward next week's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before Congress by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.

The Fed Chairman is scheduled to present his testimony on monetary policy and economic conditions to the House Banking subcommittee on domestic and international monetary policy at 1400 EDT/1800 GMT on Tuesday.
He is scheduled to present the same testimony to the Senate Banking Committee at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT on Wednesday.

"The May U.S. trade figures could affect early morning trading on Friday but as you move into the afternoon, especially if we have climbed higher from current levels, you might see a little bit of profit-taking as you head into next week," said Flanagan.
"Because the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony is the pivotal event for next week. No doubt about it," he said.
In early trade, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 4/32 to 102-1/32, yielding 6.47 percent.
Three-, six- and year-bill rates were all unchanged at 5.05 percent, 5.09 percent and 5.21 percent, respectively.

Two-year notes were unchanged at 100-8/32, yielding 5.86 percent. Five-year notes were unchanged at 100-21/32, yielding 6.09 percent and ten-year notes were up 1/32 to 103-6/32, yielding 6.19 percent.
